overall_structure.value: Nano-bainitic (nB) microstructure formed by austenitizing S3 at 1220 °C and austempering at 350 °C, comprising bainitic ferrite laths/plates (mixed Type 1 and Type 2 nano-bainite) with blocky/film-like retained austenite (γr) between sheaves, a residual polygonal ferrite (αp) fraction (~8.2%) that could not be eliminated, and cementite-like (Fe,M)xCy carbides near the γr–bainitic ferrite boundaries. Increase of TB to 350 °C raises SD(Lt(t)) indicating a broader range of bainite thicknesses.

interaction_type.value: carbon partitioning from αp into adjacent austenite

qualitative_or_quantitative_description.value: The low C solubility of pre-existing αp leads to significant C-partitioning into the adjacent austenite (C-enrichment), locally stabilizing the adjacent austenite and inhibiting austenite–bainite transformation by raising the energy barrier around αp plates.

interaction_type.value: bainite nucleation/growth stalling at αp–austenite interfaces

qualitative_or_quantitative_description.value: Initial nucleation was observed at αp–austenite interfaces, but bainite growth could not propagate and stalled at many sites, producing transformation-free regions requiring significantly longer holding times; the S3 steel retains a noticeable αp fraction even at elevated TA.
At 270 °C the higher average εγ (0.54 %) versus ferritic phase (0.33 %) indicates pronounced dislocation accumulation in γr, forming brittle phase boundaries; (at 350 °C εγ 0.55 % ≈ εα 0.50 %).

phase_evolution.value: For S3 a modified (higher) austenitization approach (1220 °C) was adopted due to the unavoidable presence of αp (~8.2%). αp plates can serve as nucleation sites for bainite but their low C solubility causes C-partitioning and local austenite stabilization, impeding bainite nucleation and growth, leading to partially decomposed sluggish γr in some micro-regions and a distinct slow-growth stage during austempering.

interface_notes.value: The αp facilitates local carbon enrichment and stabilization of surrounding austenite, explaining the slowest bainitic transformation among the studied steels; idiomorphic/allotriomorphic ferrite plates observed by LOM.

performance_notes.value: For S3 at TB 350 °C the PSE was 11,150 MPa·% (UTS 1360 MPa, El 8.2 %). However, at 270 °C (just above Ms) ductility dropped to 2.4 % despite higher UTS (1450 MPa), giving a low PSE of ~3480 MPa·%, confirming a strength–ductility trade-off. The 8.08 wt.% Al design is detrimental to ductility at lower TB; S3 shows the slowest bainitic transformation (Bt 14,000–43,000 s).

unmapped_findings: For S3 (TA 1220 °C, TB 350 °C) the bainitic transformation finish time Bt was ~14,000 s with a 140 s incubation period; a distinctive slow bainite growth period lasting nearly 1500 s at TB 350 °C was observed (source blocks b0056, figure_006).
Product of strength and elongation (PSE) for S3 at TA 1220 °C / TB 350 °C was 11,150 MPa·% (UTS 1360 MPa × El 8.2 %) (source block b0063).

Ms of S3 austenitized at 1220 °C was 258 °C, the lowest among the studied steels, consistent with extended κ-carbide dissolution and ferrite retention enabling local carbon partitioning into austenite despite the Ms-raising tendency of its very high Al content (source blocks b0035, b0036, b0056, figure_005).

S3 (highest Al content, 8.08 wt.%) exhibited the slowest bainitic transformation of all studied steels (Bt 14,000–43,000 s depending on austempering temperature), attributed to αp promoting local carbon enrichment and stabilization of surrounding austenite (source blocks b0110, b0056).

No E2₁-type stoichiometric perovskite κ-carbide was directly observed microscopically in the study; residual κ-carbides are presumed to exist as nanoscale, embedded, non-stoichiometric L1₂-type structures due to limited Mn (~1 wt.%) (source block b0085).

The (Fe,M)xCy carbides in S3 showed a slight increase/stoichiometric shift in the TTP curve nose compared to S1 and S2 (attributed to higher Al content), which appears to have a negligible impact on the mechanical properties (source block b0079).
